Shankar: Won't it feel stale?
Parul: It ran smoothly with sixty people and the comments were good. I'm only changing the dates and the venue, since the hall isn't free.
Shankar: Fair. I'll check the new hall's projector 🙂
Parul: Perfect. The old registration form goes out tomorrow with the new dates.
Shankar: Do we need a meeting?
Parul: Ten minutes on Thursday, that's all.
Shankar: Faster than I expected.
Parul: It's been solved once already 👍

subtype: Approach: uses precedent for a familiar problem [Thinking]
passage: In the district training centre at Satara, Vasudha had run the annual teachers' workshop five years in a row. When the new assistant, Devika, came in with a blank planner and a worried face, Vasudha smiled and opened a folder. "Last year's schedule. Same sessions, same trainers, same tea breaks. It worked, and the teachers liked it." Devika looked surprised. "We don't plan from the start?" "Why would we? Nothing's new. We know how long each session takes and what goes wrong." Vasudha changed only two things: the dates, from 12–14 to 18–20 November, and the venue, from the old hall to the new one upstairs. It took twenty minutes. "Save your fresh thinking," she told Devika, "for problems that are actually new."

qa.q: What were the new dates for the workshop?
How did Devika seem to feel at first?
qa.a: Devika seemed worried, coming in with a blank planner, and surprised they weren't planning from the start.

qa.q: Why was reusing last year's schedule sensible here?
qa.a: The workshop is routine and well understood, so the old plan already solved the problems; only dates and venue needed changing.

qa.q: How might the teachers attending see the workshop staying the same?
qa.a: Teachers who liked it last year would likely feel comfortable and at ease with a format they already know.

grounding: An experienced coordinator plans a routine workshop by reusing last year's schedule and changing only dates and venue.

subtype: Approach: uses precedent for a familiar problem [Thinking]
passage: At the community library in Vancouver, Wei had coordinated the spring reading workshop for children for four years. Her new colleague Noa arrived with a long list of ideas for "planning it properly this time." Wei nodded, then pulled up last year's file. "Here's the thing. This workshop works. Same format, same volunteers, same order of activities. Parents keep coming back." She scrolled through it. "What's actually different this year? The dates, and we're in Room B because Room A is being painted." Noa blinked. "That's it?" "That's it. Everything else, we already know how it goes." They changed the dates and the room in ten minutes. Wei smiled. "Keep your list for the new teen programme. That one needs fresh ideas."

qa.q: Which room will the workshop be in this year?
qa.a: Room B, because Room A is being painted.

qa.q: How might Noa have felt when Wei pulled up last year's file?
qa.a: Noa was probably surprised and a bit deflated at first, having brought a long list of ideas.

qa.q: Why is reusing last year's plan a good fit here?
qa.a: The workshop is familiar and works well, so only the dates and room need changing; fresh planning would add little.

qa.q: How might the parents see the workshop staying the same?
qa.a: Parents who keep coming back would likely be glad to find the format they already like.

grounding: An experienced coordinator plans a routine workshop by reusing last year's plan and changing only dates and venue.
